metadata.title: Dickerson v. United States, 530 U.S. 428 (2000) (No. 99-5525)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Dickerson v. United States

Opinion filed: 2000-06-26

Docket No.: 99-5525

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 405
• 120 S. Ct. 2326
• 530 U.S. 428
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 4305

Case holding summaries:
• overruling a 1968 statute designed to abrogate Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966), because “Congress may not legislatively supersede our decisions interpreting and applying the Constitution.”
• stating that the voluntariness of confessions must be examined even after appropriate Miranda warnings
• construing 18 U.S.C. sec. 3501 and holding that Miranda and its progeny govern the admissibility of statements made during custodial interrogation in both state and federal courts
• stating that " stare decisis is not an inexorable command, particularly when we are interpreting the Constitution," but refusing to overrule precedent
• “[W]e need not go further than Miranda to decide this case.”
• upholding Miranda against legislative challenge, but declining to hold that nothing be- sides Miranda will ever “suffice to satisfy constitutional re- quirements”
• holding that Miranda announced a binding “constitutional rule” under the Fifth Amendment
• failure to give required Miranda warnings amounts to Fifth Amendment violation
• " Miranda . . . held that certain warnings must be given before a suspect's statement made during custodial interrogation could be admitted in evidence."
• holding that Miranda is “constitutionally based” and Congress could not supercede Miranda with totality-of-the-circumstances approach
• "[U]nwarned statements may not be used as evidence in the prosecution’s case in chief."
• setting out brief historical account of federal constitutional law governing the admission of confessions
• holding that Miranda established a constitutional rule
• "Over time, our cases recognized two constitutional bases for the requirement that a confession be voluntary to be admitted into evidence: the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment"
• tracing the evolution of the “due process voluntariness test” to its modern formulation, which examines “whether a defendant’s will was overborne by the circumstances surrounding the giving of a confession.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "custodial police interrogation, by its very nature, isolates and pressures the individual ..."
• providing historical account of inadmissibility of coerced confessions
• discussing the constitutional rule announced in Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436, 86 S.Ct. 1602, 16 L.Ed.2d 694 (1966)
• stating Miranda protections were constitutionally required
• stating that Miranda was a “constitutional decision of this court”
• holding that Congress could not overrule Miranda and force a return to the pre-Miranda voluntariness standard for judging the admissibility of confessions because the protections of Miranda were themselves constitutional in stature
• recounting the common-law roots and constitutional bases of the voluntariness test
• "The roots of [the traditional voluntariness test] developed in the common law, as the courts of England and then the United States recognized that coerced confessions are inherently untrustworthy."
• holding that "Congress may not legislatively supersede our decisions interpreting and applying the Constitution...."
• noting constitutional underpinnings of Miranda
• “The requirement that Miranda warnings be given does not, of course, dispense with the voluntariness inquiry.”
• “The determination [of voluntariness of a confession] depends upon a weighing of the circumstances of pressure against the power of resistance of the person confessing.” (quotation marks omitted)
• holding that Miranda announced a constitutional rule
• " Miranda has become embedded in routine police practice to the point where the warnings have become part of our national culture."
• “The requirement that Miranda warnings be given does not, of course, dispense with the voluntariness inqui- ry.”
• noting that the totality of the circumstances inquiry “is more difficult than Miranda for law enforcement officers to conform to, and for courts to apply in a consistent manner”
• “Congress may not legislatively supersede our decisions interpreting and applying the Constitution.”
• "While stare decisis is not an inex- orable command, . . . the doctrine carries such persuasive force that we have always required a departure from prece- dent to be supported by some special justification."
• "Congress retains the ultimate authority to modify or set aside any judicially created rules of evidence and procedure that are not required by the Constitution."
• indicating that the test to determine the voluntariness of a statement is distinct from the determination concerning a defendant’s waiver of his Miranda rights
• holding that because Miranda was a constitutional decision, it cannot be overruled by an act of Congress
• holding that “the protections announced in Miranda” are “constitutionally required”
• reaffirming the principle that Congress may not legislatively supersede decisions of the Supreme Court interpreting and applying the Constitution
• discussing traditional standards for determining whether a confession was involuntary
• “Miranda has become embedded in routine police practice to the point where the warnings have become part of our national culture.”
• "[T]he coercion inherent in custodial interrogation blurs the line between voluntary and involuntary statements, and thus heightens the risk that an individual will not be `accorded his privilege under the Fifth Amendment . . . not to be compelled to incriminate himself' "
• "This Court has supervisory authority over the federal courts, and we may use that authority to prescribe rules of evidence and procedure that are binding in those tribunals"
• “Miranda . . . held that certain warnings must be given before a suspect’s statement made during custodial interrogation could be admitted in evidence.”
• discussing the history of admitting inculpatory statements
• holding that Miranda was "a constitutional decision, " which "may not be in effect overruled by an Act of Congress"; " Miranda announced a constitutional rule that Congress may not supersede legislatively" (emphasis supplied)
• holding that requirements of Miranda are constitutional in nature
• holding that the warnings required by Miranda are constitutionally based, and upholding Miranda 's "core ruling that unwarned statements may not be used as evidence in the prosecution's case in chief."
• “The determination [of voluntariness of a confession] depends upon a weighing of the circumstances of pressure against the power of resistance of the person confessing.” (quotation marks omitted)
• failure to give Miranda warnings
• discussing § 3501(b) and stating " Miranda and its progeny ... govern the admissibility of statements made during custodial interrogation"
